name: Graham diet

card.summary: An 1830s American vegetarian regimen of coarse whole-grain bread, water and plain living, promoted by Sylvester Graham for health and vigor.
card.note: Historical movement; Graham's wider claims are not accepted by modern medicine.

quick.overview:
The Graham diet was a regimen promoted by minister Sylvester Graham in the 1830s: vegetarian eating built on bread from coarsely ground whole wheat, pure water, and avoidance of spices and other stimulants. Followers aimed for health, vitality and clear-headed vigor.

Its appearance angle is the old idea that plain whole foods and a hygienic lifestyle produce a healthier body. Graham flour and graham crackers grew out of the movement, though Graham did not invent or profit from them.
quick.how: Practice meant home-baked coarse bread, a vegetarian table, water, cold baths, hard mattresses and ventilated rooms; Grahamite boarding houses enforced the rules.
quick.risks: Modern accounts note some of Graham's other claims, such as diet curbing impure thoughts and disease, are outdated; a whole-grain vegetarian diet itself is a common modern pattern.

lead: The Graham diet, or Grahamism, was a health regimen promoted by Sylvester Graham (1794-1851) centered on a vegetarian diet of bread baked from coarsely ground flour, pure water, and avoidance of spices and other 'stimulants'.[1] It was paired with cold baths, hard mattresses and fresh air.[1]

Graham believed that following natural law would keep people healthy and saw his approach as an early form of preventive medicine.[1][2] Followers reportedly fared better in the 1832 New York cholera epidemic, which boosted his popularity.[1]
The movement left graham flour, graham bread and graham crackers, products created for his followers.[2]

chain: Whole-grain vegetarian diet and hygienic habits
angle.text: Graham's followers pursued vigor and wellness through diet and living habits. Appearance benefits were a general part of that health-reform outlook rather than a stated cosmetic goal.

infobox: Vegetarian; coarse home-baked wheat bread; water

paras: Graham advised homemade bread from coarse flour, water, vegetarianism with eggs allowed at breakfast in boarding houses, and no spices; he also recommended cold baths, hard mattresses and open windows.[1]

Influenced by Broussais's 1826 physiology, Graham concluded diet strongly shapes health; his preaching spread during the 1826-1837 cholera pandemic.[1][2] He published a bread treatise in 1837 and Lectures on the Science of Human Life in 1839, and in 1850 helped found the American Vegetarian Society.[1] Lectures prompted riots in Providence (1833), Portland (1834) and Boston (1837), with butchers, bakers and parts of the medical profession opposed.[1] Commercial graham crackers developed from about 1880 and were mass-produced by the National Biscuit Company from 1898.[2] John Harvey Kellogg was among those influenced by him.[1]
Graham is often called the father of American vegetarianism and cited by food historians as an early food faddist; after his death some vegetarians distanced themselves from Grahamism.[1]
